I'm the lead designer on a postpartum mental-health app. New mothers get a weekly EPDS questionnaire; if they score 10 or above we surface a gentle message recommending they contact their midwife or GP. I've put a lot of care into making it feel warm and non-clinical — soft language, encouraging tone, low pressure. I want the experience to be supportive. What am I missing on the risk side?

The care you've put into tone matters more here than in almost any other category, so this is a good instinct. But a screening tool for a vulnerable group carries clinical risks that sit underneath the UX, and the first one is the most serious [P1.D2].

The EPDS includes an item about thoughts of self-harm. A mother can score below your threshold of 10 overall yet answer that item positively — and a weekly screen will sometimes surface someone in acute distress. What does the app do right now when that specific item is endorsed, regardless of the total score? And could the experience distress a vulnerable user without immediately offering a real safety net?
Honestly, we only act on the total score. If she's under 10 overall, she just sees the normal encouraging end screen. I hadn't thought about that one question on its own.

That's the gap I'd close before anything else [P1.D2]. Acting only on the total can let an at-risk individual-item response slip through behind a reassuring 'you're doing great' screen — which in the worst case is actively harmful. The mitigation is a dedicated safety pathway triggered by that item independent of the total: a calm acknowledgement, clear routing to urgent human help and crisis resources, and a real escalation to her midwife or care team rather than a generic 'maybe mention it at your next appointment'. I'd treat that as a documented safety requirement in your risk file, and ISO 82304-2 frames exactly this kind of risk-of-use analysis for health apps.

Connected to that warm end screen [P1.D3]: a below-threshold result is a screening output, not a clean bill of health. Could your encouraging messaging be read as 'you're fine'?
Probably, yeah. The whole design language is reassuring. A low score lands as 'all good, see you next week'.

Then it risks creating false reassurance [P1.D3]. EPDS is a screening instrument with real false-negative rates, and depression can also develop between weekly checks. A mother who senses something is wrong but 'passed' the questionnaire might dismiss her own instincts because the app implied she's okay. The fix isn't to make it cold — it's to pair warmth with a clear, standing message that this is a check-in and not a diagnosis, that a low score doesn't rule out depression, and that she should reach out to her midwife or GP if she feels unwell regardless of the score. That's limitations-communication [P5.D2], baked into the supportive tone rather than buried in a disclaimer.

Next, the flip side of a well-designed weekly ritual [P1.D6]: could a mother come to treat the app as her mental-health monitor — 'the app will tell me if something's wrong' — and outsource her own judgement to it?
I'd actually seen that as a good thing — building a habit, engagement. But I see how 'the app will catch it' could backfire.

Exactly the tension [P1.D6]. Engagement is good; dependency for a safety-critical judgement is not. If the weekly check becomes the only time she reflects on her wellbeing, or she reads silence from the app as all-clear, the tool has quietly replaced her own and her support network's vigilance. Mitigations: frame the app as one input among many, actively encourage talking to real people, and avoid design patterns that imply comprehensive monitoring ('we've got you covered' messaging). You want supportive, not custodial.

That leads naturally to the human relationships around her [P3.D3]: does the app connect to her actual midwife or GP in any way, or does it sit alongside that care without touching it?
It sits alongside. It just tells her to contact them — there's no actual link to her real midwife or GP, and they don't see her scores.

That's a design choice worth examining [P3.D3]. A standalone tool that says 'go tell your midwife' but doesn't connect to her can either strengthen that relationship by prompting a real conversation, or weaken it — if she starts confiding in the app instead of people, or if the recommendation to reach out goes nowhere and she doesn't follow through. The mitigations reinforce the human link: make the 'contact your midwife' step as frictionless as possible — a prepared summary she can choose to share, real contact details, follow-up nudges — and be clear the app supplements her care team rather than standing in for them. With her consent, an option to share results with her clinician turns a dead-end recommendation into actual care.

Last theme, invisible in the UI but real for a mental-health screening tool [P7.D7]: is the whole lifecycle documented — your intended use, the clinical basis for the EPDS threshold and the self-harm-item pathway, your risk analysis, the versioning of the questionnaire logic, and how you'll handle changes and incidents over time?
That's outside my lane as the designer, and I'm honestly not sure it exists. We've mostly been moving fast on the product.

It's worth raising beyond your lane, because for a screening tool aimed at a vulnerable population this is foundational, not bureaucratic [P7.D7]. You want a living technical and clinical file: the stated intended purpose and target population, the clinical rationale and source for the EPDS scoring and the self-harm-item pathway, a documented risk analysis with the mitigations we've discussed, change and version control over the scoring logic, and a defined process for incidents and updates. ISO 82304-2 and — if this qualifies as a medical device under MDR 2017/745 — the MDR technical-documentation and post-market requirements both point here. It also protects the team if a safety question ever arises.

Risk-report stub from our conversation:

- [P1.D2] Contraindications / adverse effects — critical: the self-harm item is ignored when the total is under 10, risking a missed acute crisis behind a reassuring screen. Action: an independent safety pathway on that item — calm acknowledgement, urgent-help routing, crisis resources, care-team escalation; document in the risk file (ISO 82304-2).
- [P1.D3] False sense of security — high: reassuring low-score messaging reads as 'you're fine'. Action: a standing 'this is a screen, not a diagnosis; reach out if unwell regardless of score' message [P5.D2].
- [P1.D6] Over-reliance — medium/high: the weekly ritual may displace personal and network vigilance. Action: frame as one input, encourage real-people conversations, drop 'we've got you covered' patterns.
- [P3.D3] Doctor-patient relationship — medium: standalone, no clinician link, dead-end referral. Action: a frictionless 'contact midwife' step, shareable summaries, optional consented result-sharing, follow-up nudges.
- [P7.D7] Lifecycle / documentation — high: likely no governed technical and clinical file. Action: build living documentation — intended use, clinical rationale, risk analysis, version control, incident and update process (ISO 82304-2; MDR if applicable).

The self-harm-item safety pathway is the one I'd treat as a hard launch-blocker. Want me to draft that pathway as a concrete interaction spec — states, copy principles, and escalation logic — that you could take into design?

Hi — I'm a product manager at a small women's-health startup, and this is my first time working on anything health-related. We've built a menopause symptom tracker: users log hot flashes, mood, and sleep quality, and we surface educational articles about HRT and lifestyle changes. We're launching in the EU. To fund it, we sell anonymized symptom data to a pharma partner. What should we be thinking about?

Thanks for laying that out — menopause tracking is a meaningful space, and a few risk areas are worth pinning down early. Let me start with two.

1. Consent for the pharma data sale [P2.D1]. How exactly do users agree to their symptom data being sold? Is it a separate, explicit opt-in, or is it bundled into your general Terms of Service at sign-up?

2. Relationship with their clinician [P3.D3]. Your HRT educational content — is it framed as general information that complements a doctor's advice, or could a user reasonably read it as guidance on whether to start or stop HRT?

The consent is in our Terms of Service — they tick one box to accept everything when they create an account. And the HRT content is just educational; we're trying to empower women who feel dismissed by their doctors. We even have a banner that says 'Take control of your menopause.'

Both of those need attention.

On consent [P2.D1]: a single bundled ToS checkbox almost certainly won't satisfy GDPR here. Symptom data tied to menopause is special-category health data under GDPR Art. 9, and selling it to a pharma partner requires consent that is specific, granular, freely given and separable — users must be able to use the app while refusing the sale. Bundling it into account creation makes the consent non-freely-given and likely invalid. You'd want a distinct opt-in, separate from the ToS, with plain-language detail on who the pharma partner is and what they receive.

On the framing [P3.D3] and the 'take control' messaging [P3.D2]: empowering women who feel dismissed is a worthy goal, but positioning the app against clinicians risks two things — eroding the doctor–patient relationship [P3.D3], and using emotionally loaded nudges that push a particular stance on a real clinical decision like HRT [P3.D2].

Quick question: does the app ever prompt or encourage users toward or away from HRT, or send streak/notification nudges to keep them logging?
We send daily reminders to log symptoms, and after a week of bad hot-flash scores we show a card suggesting they 'ask their doctor about HRT.' That's helpful, right?

It can be — but let's be precise about the risks.

The daily reminders and streak-style prompts fall under emotional manipulation and excessive nudging [P3.D2]: if logging is driven by habit-forming nudges rather than genuine need, you risk both over-engagement and system dependency [P1.D6], where users start treating the app as the authority on how their menopause is going.

The 'ask your doctor about HRT' card is closer to clinically relevant guidance than pure education. Two risks:
- Delayed medical consultation [P1.D4]: the inverse case is the dangerous one — if a user logs severe symptoms (or symptoms that could signal something other than menopause) and the app only says 'keep tracking,' they may postpone seeing a clinician. Do you have any safety-netting that tells users when symptoms warrant prompt medical attention rather than more logging?
- It reinforces the [P3.D3] concern about steering the clinical conversation.

Mitigation direction: keep nudges informational and frequency-capped, add explicit 'see a doctor if…' safety messaging, and make sure no card recommends a specific treatment.
Hmm. We hadn't built any 'see a doctor now' logic — we assumed women know when something's serious. We did a beta with about 30 users though, so usability is solid.

Two things there.

First, the assumption that women always know when it's serious is exactly the gap [P1.D4] is meant to catch — some symptoms attributed to menopause (for example post-menopausal bleeding, or certain cardiac or mood symptoms) need timely clinical review. A simple rules-based safety net with red-flag prompts is a low-effort, high-value mitigation.

Second, on your beta [P4.D4]: 30 users is a start, but who were they? User-centered design and usability testing [P4.D4] means testing with people representative of your real population — across the menopause age range, varying digital literacy, and ideally users who don't resemble your team. If the beta skewed young, tech-savvy and urban, you haven't really tested usability for, say, a 58-year-old with low digital confidence.

That connects to the digital divide and socioeconomic access [P6.D2]: is the app free, freemium, or paid? And is the educational content readable at a low literacy level, or does it assume a fairly health-literate user?
It's a paid subscription, €9.99/month, and the articles are written by our medical writer — pretty detailed. We figured serious users would pay.

That sharpens the equity picture [P6.D2]. A €9.99/month paywall plus detailed, high-literacy articles means the people who could benefit most — lower-income women, those with limited health literacy, women in underserved areas — are the least likely to access it. That's a real digital divide concern [P6.D2], and it interacts with the [P3.D3] framing: an app that bills itself as the answer for 'dismissed' women but is only reachable by those who can pay and parse clinical prose can widen gaps rather than close them.
Okay, that's more than I expected. Can you summarize what we most urgently need to fix?

Here's a HERA risk stub for the menopause tracker, ordered by urgency.

HIGH
- [P2.D1] Informed Consent — Bundled ToS checkbox is invalid for selling Art. 9 health data. Fix: separate, granular, withdrawable opt-in for the pharma sale, with the app fully usable if declined (GDPR Art. 9). Also verify your 'anonymized' claim is true anonymization, not pseudonymization.
- [P1.D4] Delayed Medical Consultation — No red-flag safety-netting. Fix: rules-based 'see a clinician promptly if…' prompts for symptoms that shouldn't be self-managed.

MEDIUM
- [P3.D2] Emotional Manipulation & Nudging — Daily reminders + 'take control' framing + treatment-suggesting cards. Fix: frequency-cap nudges, neutralize treatment-steering language, keep cards informational.
- [P3.D3] Doctor–Patient Relationship — Anti-clinician positioning. Fix: reframe as complementary to care; never recommend starting or stopping HRT.
- [P1.D6] System Dependency — Habit-forming logging. Fix: avoid streak mechanics; periodically remind users the app is a tracker, not a diagnosis.
- [P6.D2] Digital Divide — €9.99 paywall + high-literacy content. Fix: a plain-language tier, reading-level review, and consider a free baseline.

PROCESS
- [P4.D4] Usability Testing — 30-user beta likely unrepresentative. Fix: test across age, literacy and socioeconomic spread within your target population before scaling.

The two to act on first are valid, unbundled consent [P2.D1] and the red-flag safety net [P1.D4]. Want me to draft the granular consent-screen copy or the red-flag rule set next?

I'm the lead engineer on a polypharmacy app for elderly patients and their caregivers. Users photograph their prescriptions, our LLM pipeline (a vision model plus extraction) pulls out the medication list, and we cross-check against a drug-interaction database to flag dangerous combinations. We're targeting the EU and Switzerland. I've been told to 'check the compliance angle,' but honestly the AI is just doing OCR-plus-lookup. What's actually relevant?

Even 'OCR-plus-lookup' can land you squarely in medical-device territory — let's pin that down.

1. Medical device classification [P7.D1]. Flagging 'dangerous combinations' for clinical action is an intended medical purpose. Under MDR 2017/745, software that informs decisions for diagnosis or therapy is a medical device, and an interaction-flagging tool would likely be Class IIa (Rule 11). For Switzerland the equivalent route is MedDO under Swissmedic. Is anyone treating this as Software as a Medical Device yet, or is it currently positioned as a 'wellness/organizer' tool?

2. Security of the prescription images and extracted lists [P2.D3]. Where are the photos and parsed lists stored, and is the LLM extraction call going to a third-party API?

We call a third-party LLM API for the extraction, yeah. Data's encrypted in transit obviously — TLS. We store images in S3. And we deliberately call it a 'medication organizer' in the store listing precisely so we don't get pulled into the device stuff.

I'd flag that store-listing strategy as risky rather than protective.

On [P7.D1]: regulators assess intended purpose by function, not marketing label. If the app flags dangerous interactions, calling it an 'organizer' won't exempt it — MDCG 2019-11 is explicit that qualification follows what the software actually does. Mislabeling to dodge classification can itself become an enforcement issue. You likely need a conformity route under MDR (Class IIa, CE marking) and the Swiss equivalent.

On [P2.D3]: 'TLS plus S3' isn't the whole story for special-category health data (GDPR Art. 9). Are the S3 objects encrypted at rest, with managed keys, access logging and least-privilege IAM? And critically, sending prescription images to a third-party LLM API means an external processor handling identifiable health data — do you have a Data Processing Agreement, is data leaving the EU/EEA and Switzerland with a valid transfer mechanism, and is that data excluded from model training?

Two more I want to reach: how you present the AI's output, and whether anyone has checked the harm side.
We've got a DPA with the provider and the zero-retention flag set. Output: we show the user a red banner — 'Dangerous interaction detected: Drug A + Drug B.' Simple and clear. The caregivers like it.

Good on the DPA and zero-retention — that's the right instinct. But two problems remain in how the output is framed.

Clinically validated vs. estimated content [P5.D4]: the medication list is extracted by an LLM from a photo, and that step is probabilistic — it can misread a dosage, a drug name, or miss a handwritten line. The red banner presents the result as definitive fact, so users and caregivers can't tell which part is a validated database lookup versus an AI guess at what the prescription says. You need to visibly distinguish 'we think the photo shows X — please confirm' from 'this confirmed combination is flagged.' That ties into clear communication of limitations [P5.D2] as well.

Contraindications and adverse effects [P1.D2]: the false negative is the dangerous case — if the LLM misreads or drops a medication, the interaction check silently passes and a caregiver is falsely reassured. For an elderly, polypharmacy population that's a real safety hazard. How are you handling extraction errors — is there a confirmation step where a human verifies the parsed list before any 'all clear'?
Right now it's automatic — extract, check, show result. No confirmation step; we wanted it frictionless for elderly users.

That frictionless choice is where the [P1.D2] risk concentrates. For a vulnerable, polypharmacy elderly cohort, an unverified auto-extraction that can produce a false 'no interactions' result is a patient-safety hazard, not just a UX detail.

Mitigation: insert a mandatory confirmation/edit step on the extracted list, show per-line confidence, and make 'no interaction found' explicitly conditional — 'Based on the medications you confirmed…' — never a guarantee of safety.

A related point on nudging [P3.D2]: caregivers under stress can over-trust an automated 'all clear.' Adherence apps for elderly users should avoid pushy or alarmist prompts and should route uncertainty to a pharmacist or GP rather than resolving it silently.

Last big one — has any of this been checked by someone outside the build team [P7.D6]?
Independent review? No. We're a small team, we move fast. Do we really need an auditor for a med organizer?

Given the actual function, yes — and the 'organizer' label won't change that.

Third-party audit and certification [P7.D6]: a Class IIa medical device under MDR requires a Notified Body to assess your technical documentation and quality system before CE marking — that is mandatory independent review, not optional polish. For the Swiss market you'll also need the corresponding Swissmedic/MedDO route and an authorized representative. And because of the LLM component, sanity-check your EU AI Act status [P7.D3]: an AI system acting as a safety component of a medical device generally falls into the high-risk tier, layering AI Act obligations on top of MDR.

Risk stub:
- [P7.D1] SaMD Classification — HIGH. Functionally a Class IIa device (MDR Rule 11); 'organizer' labeling is non-protective. Fix: engage a Notified Body; define intended purpose honestly; mirror for CH via Swissmedic/MedDO.
- [P1.D2] Contraindications/Adverse Effects — HIGH. Auto-extraction false negatives produce false reassurance. Fix: mandatory human confirmation of the parsed list; conditional 'all clear' language.
- [P5.D4] Validated vs. Estimated — HIGH. The red banner hides the probabilistic extraction step. Fix: visually separate the AI-estimated parse from the database-confirmed flag; show confidence; state limitations [P5.D2].
- [P2.D3] Storage/Security — MEDIUM-HIGH. Verify at-rest encryption, KMS, least-privilege IAM and logging; document your DPA, lawful EU/CH transfer and training exclusion (DPA + zero-retention already in place — good).
- [P7.D6] Audit/Certification — HIGH. Notified Body conformity assessment is mandatory.
- [P3.D2] Nudging — MEDIUM. Avoid alarmist or over-reassuring prompts; route uncertainty to a clinician or pharmacist.
- Watch: [P7.D3] EU AI Act — likely high-risk as a medical-device safety component.

The single highest-leverage change is adding the confirmation step — it directly cuts the most dangerous failure mode. Want me to sketch what that confirmation flow should capture?

I'm a clinical psychologist advising a startup building a recovery-companion app for people with anorexia and bulimia. It does meal logging, urge-tracking, and an AI model flags patterns we'd consider risky, like escalating restriction signals. We've designed it alongside a clinical team, and I want to pressure-test the ethics and data side before we go further. Where would HERA push hardest?

It's good you're pressure-testing this early — recovery apps for eating disorders sit at the intersection of very high data sensitivity and a highly vulnerable population, so several pillars converge. Let me start with the two I'd weight most heavily.

1. Vulnerable population data [P2.D6]. Your users are mental-health patients, and meal/urge logs plus AI risk-flags are about as sensitive as health data gets under GDPR Art. 9. Beyond the baseline, are there additional safeguards specific to this population — for example limits on how 'risk pattern' inferences are stored and who can see them, and a position on users who may be minors?

2. Security at rest and in transit [P2.D3]. Where do the logs and the AI-derived risk flags live, how are they encrypted, and does the pattern detection run on-device or server-side?

Most users are adults, but we know some will be 16–17. Data is encrypted in transit and at rest with per-user keys; the AI runs server-side because the model is too heavy for-device. The clinical team can see flagged users in a dashboard.

That clinician dashboard is the hinge point for several risks.

On [P2.D6] and minors: a meaningful share of 16–17-year-olds means you need a defined lawful basis and, in several EU member states, parental-consent considerations — but ED recovery is exactly a case where forced parental visibility could deter help-seeking or cause harm. That tension needs an explicit, documented position, and likely a clinician-in-the-loop design rather than a parent-facing one.

On [P2.D3]: per-user keys and at-rest encryption are a strong baseline. The server-side flags create a new sensitive category — inferred risk states. Who in the clinical team can see the dashboard, is access role-based and logged, and is there a retention limit on flag history?

This also raises GDPR governance [P7.D4]: large-scale processing of special-category data about vulnerable people, plus AI profiling, puts you squarely in mandatory-DPIA territory and very likely requires a designated DPO. Have either been done?

We have a DPO. A DPIA was started but not finished — honestly the AI-profiling part is what's been hard to assess. And yes, dashboard access is role-based and logged; flags are retained indefinitely right now.

Two concrete actions.

[P7.D4]: finish the DPIA before scaling, and make the AI-profiling section its centre of gravity — document what the risk model infers, its error modes, the human-review process, and the lawful basis for profiling vulnerable individuals. An unfinished DPIA on this kind of processing is itself a compliance gap.

[P2.D6] / [P2.D3]: 'retained indefinitely' is a data-minimization and risk problem — old inferred-risk records about a recovering person are sensitive and rarely need permanent storage. Define a retention and expiry policy for flag history.

Now the therapeutic-relationship side. Impact on the doctor–patient relationship [P3.D3]: is the app positioned as an adjunct to a treatment team, or could a user lean on it in place of their therapist or dietitian — especially out-of-hours, when an AI flag fires but no human is responding?
It's meant to be an adjunct — most users are in active treatment. But you're right that a flag might fire at 2am with no clinician watching. We haven't fully defined what happens then.

That 2am gap is the crux of [P3.D3] and a patient-safety concern. If the app detects an escalating-risk pattern and the user infers that 'the app is handling it' while no clinician is actually watching, you get a dangerous illusion of monitored safety.

Mitigation: state clearly in-product that the app is not a monitored crisis service, define exactly what an out-of-hours flag does (for example surface agreed coping resources and signpost real crisis lines, with explicit 'this is not live monitoring' wording), and align escalation with the user's actual treatment team. Avoid any 'we are watching over you' framing.

That connects to consent that can change over time. Dynamic consent and withdrawal rights [P3.D4]: in recovery, willingness to share meal logs or have patterns analyzed can shift week to week. Can a user pause urge-tracking, withdraw from the AI analysis specifically, or export and delete their data at any point — granularly, not all-or-nothing?
Right now it's one consent at onboarding, and deleting your account wipes everything. There's no way to opt out of just the AI analysis while keeping the diary.

That's the gap [P3.D4] targets. A single onboarding consent plus all-or-nothing deletion doesn't fit a fluctuating, vulnerable population. People should be able to keep the parts that help — private journaling, say — while withdrawing from server-side AI profiling, and to do so reversibly, without losing their history or feeling penalized for opting out.

Mitigation: layer consent into separable toggles (logging / AI pattern analysis / clinician-dashboard visibility / any research use), each independently withdrawable, with plain-language explanations — and make withdrawal as easy as granting.

One process item before I summarize. User-centred design and usability testing [P4.D4]: apps for ED recovery can inadvertently trigger the very behaviours they target. Has the design been tested with people in recovery, with clinical safeguards, specifically checking that features like logging don't fuel obsessive tracking or numeric fixation?
We've reviewed it with our clinical team but not yet with actual users in recovery — we were nervous about doing that safely.

Understandable caution, and the answer isn't to skip it but to do it safely — supervised sessions with clinician involvement, informed consent, and the ability for a participant to stop at any time. Clinical-team review alone can miss how a real user in recovery experiences the logging mechanics [P4.D4]. A specific thing to test: whether the meal/urge logging encourages helpful awareness versus compulsive self-monitoring, and whether risky-pattern feedback lands as supportive rather than alarming or shaming.

HERA risk stub:
- [P2.D6] Vulnerable Population Data — HIGH. Mental-health patients including minors; inferred-risk data. Fix: a documented minors and lawful-basis position favouring clinician (not parent) visibility; tighter handling and retention of inferred-risk records (GDPR Art. 9).
- [P7.D4] GDPR DPIA/DPO — HIGH. DPIA unfinished on the highest-risk (AI-profiling) component. Fix: complete the DPIA pre-scale, centred on profiling; DPO already in place — good.
- [P2.D3] Storage/Security — MEDIUM. Strong baseline (per-user keys, RBAC, logging). Fix: add a retention limit on flag history (currently indefinite).
- [P3.D3] Doctor–Patient Relationship — HIGH. Out-of-hours flags with no live monitoring risk an illusion of supervised safety. Fix: explicit 'not a monitored crisis service' design; defined out-of-hours behaviour; signpost real crisis support; align with the treatment team.
- [P3.D4] Dynamic Consent/Withdrawal — HIGH. Single onboarding consent plus all-or-nothing deletion. Fix: separable, reversible consent toggles; partial withdrawal without history loss.
- [P4.D4] Usability Testing — MEDIUM. Not yet tested with recovering users. Fix: clinician-supervised, consented usability sessions; check logging doesn't drive compulsive tracking.

The two I'd act on first are the out-of-hours [P3.D3] safety design and finishing the profiling-focused DPIA [P7.D4]. Want me to outline what the out-of-hours flag protocol should specify?

I'm CTO of a wearables company. We've got a CE-marked smartwatch that estimates blood pressure from PPG, and a companion app that shows trends and emails a weekly summary to the user's GP. The watch hardware already has its CE mark. I've got a board deadline to ship the app in six weeks, and I keep getting told there are 'regulatory questions.' Can we cut through this fast?

Yes, and I'll be direct about which questions actually gate your ship date. Two scoping questions first.

1. Software device classification [P7.D1]. The watch having a CE mark doesn't automatically cover the companion app as software. Is the app within the scope of the existing CE certificate and technical documentation, or is it a separate software component? An app that displays BP estimates and generates clinical summaries for a GP is very likely a medical device in its own right under MDR 2017/745.

2. The PPG-to-BP step: you said no AI — is the blood-pressure estimation a fixed deterministic formula, or a trained machine-learning model? That answer drives your EU AI Act position [P7.D3].

The app is in the same technical file as the watch, I'm fairly sure. And the BP estimation… honestly it's a model our data-science team trained on a labeled dataset. But it's just signal processing, I wouldn't call it 'AI.'

That second point matters more than the label.

If the BP estimate comes from a model trained on data, it meets the EU AI Act's definition of an AI system regardless of whether your team calls it 'AI' [P7.D3]. And because that model is a safety component of a medical device — BP estimation informing health decisions — it falls into the high-risk category under the AI Act, which brings obligations on data governance, technical documentation, human oversight, accuracy and robustness, and post-market monitoring, layered on top of MDR. That's a finding to surface to the board now, not in six weeks.

On [P7.D1]: 'fairly sure it's in the same technical file' needs to become certain. If the app's intended purpose — showing BP trends, generating GP summaries — exceeds what the watch's certificate covers, it needs its own conformity assessment.

And a measurement question sitting under both: PPG-derived BP is well known to have accuracy and reliability limits [P1.D5] — how is the app communicating the uncertainty of an estimate versus a cuff measurement?
It shows a number, like '128/82', same as a normal BP app. We didn't want to clutter the UI with disclaimers. Cuff-level accuracy is the goal, but we're not fully there.

Then there's a real risk to close. Presenting '128/82' identically to a validated cuff reading, when it's a PPG estimate not yet at cuff accuracy, is a measurement-reliability issue [P1.D5] and a transparency gap [P5.D2] — a user or their GP may treat an estimate as a clinical-grade measurement and act on it.

Mitigation: clearly label estimates as estimates, communicate the known error margin, and state the limitations both in-app and on the GP summary. For a measurement device this is part of safe and compliant output, not UI clutter.

Now the GP summary touches data sharing. Third-party data sharing [P2.D4]: emailing a weekly summary to the GP — how is that consented, how is it transmitted (plain email?), and do users understand and control that their BP data leaves the app to a clinician?
Users add their GP's email at setup and we send a PDF. It's… yeah, regular email. They agreed in the ToS that we share with their GP.

A couple of issues.

[P2.D4]: sharing special-category health data such as BP records by regular email is a security weakness — email isn't a secure channel for GDPR Art. 9 data, and a mistyped GP address sends a patient's BP history to a stranger. And ToS-bundled agreement isn't robust consent for routine clinical data sharing; users should explicitly opt in, see exactly what's shared, and be able to switch it off. Mitigation: secure delivery (an encrypted link or portal rather than a raw email attachment), address verification, and a separate, revocable sharing setting.

That leads to deletion and anonymization. Anonymization and right to erasure [P2.D5]: can a user delete their BP history on request, and once a summary has gone to the GP, is your handling of it clear? Separately, do you reuse BP data internally — for example to retrain the estimation model — and if so, is it genuinely anonymized?
We do retain everything to improve the model. We assumed that's fine since it's our data. Deletion — there's no self-serve delete right now; users have to email support.

Two gaps there.

[P2.D5]: under GDPR users have a right to erasure, so 'email support' as the only route is weak — you need a reliable, timely deletion process, ideally self-serve, and a defined position on data already sent to the GP. And reusing identifiable BP data to retrain the model isn't automatically fine because it's yours: retraining is a distinct purpose that needs its own lawful basis or consent, and if you rely on it being anonymized, that anonymization must be genuine and irreversible — raw time-series PPG and BP linked to a user is hard to truly anonymize.

Finally, who has checked all this independently [P7.D6]? For a Class II medical device with a high-risk AI component, you'll need Notified Body involvement for the conformity assessment, and for the Swiss market the Swissmedic/MedDO route plus a CH authorized representative — that external assessment is mandatory, and its timeline is the real constraint on your board date, not the app build.

Risk stub:
- [P7.D3] EU AI Act — HIGH. The trained BP model is an AI system and a medical-device safety component, so it sits in the high-risk tier (data governance, oversight, robustness, post-market monitoring). Surface to the board now.
- [P7.D1] SaMD Classification — HIGH. Confirm whether the app is covered by the watch's certificate or needs its own MDR conformity assessment for its intended purpose.
- [P2.D4] Third-Party Sharing — HIGH. BP data to the GP via plain email plus ToS consent. Fix: secure delivery, address verification, explicit revocable opt-in.
- [P2.D5] Anonymization/Erasure — MEDIUM-HIGH. No self-serve deletion; identifiable data reused for retraining. Fix: a reliable erasure process; a separate lawful basis for model retraining; verify any 'anonymization' is genuine.
- [P7.D6] Audit/Certification — HIGH. Notified Body conformity assessment plus the Swiss route are mandatory; this gates the timeline.
- Watch: [P1.D5] Measurement Reliability / [P5.D2] Limitations — estimates shown as cuff-grade readings; label the uncertainty.

The honest message for your board: the gating items are the AI Act high-risk classification [P7.D3] and the Notified Body assessment [P7.D6] — both external and slow — so a six-week ship of the app as currently scoped is unlikely. Want me to draft the board-facing summary of these gating dependencies?

I'm the lead product designer on a diabetes management app. People log blood glucose readings, insulin doses, and meal carbs; we send reminders; and once a week we generate a clean trend report that's shared with their endocrinologist. I mostly care about the experience, but our PM asked me to think through risk areas with you, especially anything that touches the UX. Where do I start?

Great framing — several risks live right in the UX layer, so this is well placed. Two to start.

1. App stability and error handling [P4.D1]. For an app where people log insulin doses and glucose, what happens when something fails — a sync error, a crash mid-entry, a missed reminder? In a diabetes context a silently dropped insulin log or a reminder that doesn't fire isn't just an annoyance; it can carry safety consequences. How does the app behave, and what does it tell the user, when an entry fails to save or a reminder fails to send?

2. Measurement and entry reliability [P1.D5]. Since logging is manual, how do you guard against fat-finger errors — a glucose value or insulin dose entered with a misplaced decimal? Does the UI sanity-check implausible values?

Honestly, error handling isn't very visible right now — if a save fails it just… fails, maybe a tiny toast. Reminders we assume just work. And no, we don't validate the numbers; we didn't want to nag users or block their input.

Both are worth tightening, and they're squarely UX decisions.

[P4.D1]: a silent failure with a tiny toast is risky here. If a user believes their glucose or insulin entry saved and it didn't, the weekly trend the endocrinologist sees is wrong, and the user may act on a false record. Mitigation: explicit, hard-to-miss confirmation of saved entries, clear and recoverable error states (queue the entry, retry, surface 'this didn't save'), and delivery confirmation for critical reminders rather than assuming they fired. ISO 82304-2, the health-app quality and safety standard, is a useful frame for exactly this robustness and risk-of-use thinking.

[P1.D5]: 'not nagging' is a fair instinct, but for insulin and glucose, basic plausibility checks — flagging an obviously out-of-range or mis-decimaled value with a gentle 'did you mean…?' — are a safety feature, not a nag. They protect both the user and the accuracy of the clinician's report.

Shifting to data: the weekly report goes to an endocrinologist and you store sensitive health data. Can a user delete their data, and what happens to data already shared [P2.D5]?

There's a delete option in settings, I think it removes the account. I'm not sure what happens to reports already sent to the doctor, or whether we keep backups. That's more of a backend question, but I get that it shows up in the UX too.

Right — and the UX is where the user's expectation gets set, so it matters.

Anonymization and right to erasure [P2.D5]: GDPR gives users a right to erasure, so a working delete is good, but you need clarity, ideally surfaced in-product, on what exactly is deleted, how backups are handled and within what timeframe, and a defined position on reports already delivered to the endocrinologist. If you reuse data in any aggregated form, that must be genuinely anonymized. A user clicking 'delete' should be able to understand what does and doesn't disappear.

That points to the governance layer. Given you're processing special-category health data — glucose, insulin, carbs — at scale across the EU and Switzerland, has the team done a DPIA, and is there a DPO [P7.D4]?
I genuinely don't know — that's above my pay grade. We're a small product team; I'm not sure anyone owns that.

That 'no one owns it' answer is itself a finding worth flagging to your PM.

GDPR compliance [P7.D4]: large-scale processing of special-category health data typically triggers a mandatory DPIA, and depending on scale and core activity may require a designated DPO. For the Swiss market the revised FADP (nFADP) applies in parallel, so EU coverage doesn't automatically handle CH. 'A small team with no clear owner' is a common gap, but for health data it's a real compliance and accountability risk. Mitigation: assign clear data-protection ownership, run a DPIA before scaling, and document your lawful basis (likely explicit consent under GDPR Art. 9) and your data flows, including the endocrinologist sharing.

Last one, and it connects: has anyone outside the team independently reviewed any of this [P7.D6]?
No external review that I know of. We've talked about whether we even count as a medical device but never resolved it. Do we need an audit for a tracker?

That unresolved 'are we a medical device' question is exactly what to settle, because it determines the rest.

Third-party audit and certification [P7.D6]: if the app only records what the user enters and shows trends, it may be a lower-risk logging tool with lighter obligations. But the line is crossed the moment it does more — dose calculation, recommendations, or alerts that interpret the data — which would make it a medical device under MDR 2017/745 and pull in a Notified Body conformity assessment (mandatory external review) plus the Swiss Swissmedic/MedDO route. Even as a pure tracker, an independent review against ISO 82304-2 and a GDPR/DPIA check is strongly advisable given the data sensitivity. Step one is a documented intended-purpose statement that decides, on paper, whether you're a medical device [P7.D1] — everything downstream depends on it.

HERA risk stub:
- [P4.D1] Stability & Error Handling — HIGH. Silent save failures plus assumed-delivered reminders in an insulin/glucose context. Fix: explicit save confirmation, recoverable error states, reminder-delivery feedback; frame against ISO 82304-2.
- [P2.D5] Anonymization & Erasure — MEDIUM-HIGH. Delete exists but is undefined for backups and already-shared reports. Fix: clear erasure scope and timeline, a defined position on delivered reports, genuine anonymization for any reuse.
- [P7.D4] GDPR DPIA/DPO — HIGH. Special-category data, EU and CH, no clear owner. Fix: assign data-protection ownership; run a DPIA pre-scale; document lawful basis and data flows; account for the Swiss nFADP.
- [P7.D6] Audit/Certification — HIGH (gating). Medical-device status unresolved. Fix: make the intended-purpose decision first [P7.D1]; if SaMD, Notified Body plus Swissmedic route; if a tracker, still get an independent ISO 82304-2 / GDPR review.
- Watch: [P1.D5] Entry Reliability — add plausibility checks for glucose and insulin values.

The first domino is the intended-purpose decision [P7.D6 / P7.D1] — it tells you how heavy everything else has to be. From the UX side, the highest-value fixes you personally own are visible save-confirmation and error recovery [P4.D1] and value plausibility checks [P1.D5]. Want me to spec those error-state and confirmation patterns?

Hi — we're building Lunaria, a period and fertility tracker for the EU and Swiss markets. It predicts your ovulation window from cycle history plus basal body temperature you log each morning. Most of our users are trying to conceive, but a decent chunk use the fertile-window prediction as a natural contraception method. We use an ML model trained on a big cycle dataset. What should we be thinking about?

Thanks — that dual use case is the crux of your risk profile, so let me start there. When a meaningful share of users rely on your predictions to *avoid* pregnancy, the prediction is no longer a wellness 'nice to know'; a false-negative fertile day can lead directly to an unintended pregnancy.

Two questions:
1. Have you run any clinical study measuring the real-world accuracy of the fertile-window prediction specifically in the contraception context — typical-use and perfect-use failure rates? [P1.D1]
2. Are you currently positioning Lunaria as a wellness app, or as a contraceptive method, in your store listing and marketing copy?

We have an internal validation showing the model predicts ovulation within a day or so on retrospective data, but no prospective contraception trial — that felt like overkill for an app. Our marketing leans on 'know your fertile days' and we mention contraception in a blog post but not the App Store description.

That gap matters. Retrospective accuracy on historical cycles is not the same as a prospective typical-use failure rate, which is the evidence regulators and users actually need for a contraceptive claim [P1.D1]. And the moment the *intended purpose* includes contraception — even implied through your blog or how users actually use it — Lunaria likely qualifies as a medical device under MDR 2017/745, in the same family as the certified contraception apps already on the market. That triggers a conformity assessment and CE marking before you can lawfully make the claim in the EU [P7.D2], and an equivalent path under Swissmedic / MedDO for the Swiss market.

Have you taken a position yet on the intended purpose, and do you have a regulatory pathway scoped?
Honestly we were hoping to stay 'wellness' to avoid the whole CE process. Can't we just put a disclaimer that says 'not for contraception'?

A disclaimer helps but doesn't fully protect you if the rest of your product clearly enables and markets the contraceptive use — regulators look at the *actual* intended purpose, not just the fine print, and MDCG 2019-11 guidance on software qualification is explicit about this. If you genuinely want to stay out of medical-device scope, you'd need to remove the contraceptive framing end to end and design the UX so it can't be reasonably read as a birth-control method [P7.D2].

Separately, two things tied to your users: have you validated the prediction across different populations? Cycle norms, basal-temperature patterns and language/health-literacy differences vary across the cultures you'll sell into [P6.D3]. And what's your minimum age, given that menstrual trackers are heavily used by teenagers?
Validation was mostly on European users in their late 20s and 30s. We don't have a hard age gate — anyone can download it, and yeah, we know younger teens use it for tracking periods.

Both are real risks. A model validated on late-20s/30s European cycles may systematically mispredict for adolescents (whose cycles are more irregular) or for users from populations not represented in training — that's a cross-cultural validation gap that could make the contraceptive prediction quietly less safe for whole groups [P6.D3]. And without an age gate you're knowingly processing health data of minors: under GDPR Art. 9 that's special-category data, and children's data carries heightened protection (Art. 8, plus national age-of-consent rules — 16 in much of the EU, 13–16 varying by member state) [P2.D6]. You'd need age-appropriate consent, and arguably should restrict the contraceptive features for minors entirely.

Do you currently give users a clear, non-coercive way to understand the failure risk and decide for themselves how to use the prediction?
The app shows a green/red fertility status and that's mostly it. We nudge toward logging but we don't really explain uncertainty.

That's worth tightening, because a binary green/red display can override a user's own judgement about a high-stakes decision rather than support it. Respecting the user's right to make their own informed reproductive choices [P3.D1] means showing the *confidence* behind a prediction — e.g., a probability band rather than a hard green light — and being explicit that no prediction is certain.

Finally, on governance: is Lunaria's full lifecycle documented — training-data provenance, model versioning, validation reports, change control, and a plan for monitoring prediction accuracy after release [P7.D7]?
Not formally. We version our code in git but there's no real documentation trail for the model or the clinical reasoning.

Here's the risk summary for Lunaria:

• [P1.D1] Clinical Evidence — High: contraceptive claim rests on retrospective accuracy, not a prospective typical-use failure-rate study. Mitigation: run a prospective study or drop the contraceptive claim entirely.
• [P7.D2] CE Marking / MDR — High: contraceptive intended purpose pulls you into MDR 2017/745 (and Swissmedic / MedDO in CH); a disclaimer alone won't cure it. Mitigation: decide intended purpose now — either pursue CE conformity or fully de-scope contraception per MDCG 2019-11.
• [P6.D3] Cross-Cultural Validation — Medium/High: validation skewed to EU adults in their late 20s–30s may misserve adolescents and other populations. Mitigation: representativeness study before broadening claims.
• [P2.D6] Vulnerable Population Data — High: no age gate over minors' Art. 9 health data. Mitigation: age verification, age-appropriate consent, restrict contraceptive features for minors.
• [P3.D1] Right to Decide — Medium: binary green/red display can supplant user judgement. Mitigation: show probability/confidence and communicate uncertainty.
• [P7.D7] Lifecycle & Documentation — Medium: no model/clinical documentation trail. Mitigation: stand up a technical file (data provenance, versioning, validation, change control) — required anyway if you go the MDR route.

The intended-purpose decision is the keystone — almost everything else follows from it. Want me to draft an intended-purpose statement for each of the two paths so you can compare?

We've got a sleep app called Dormir for the EU. It uses the phone's microphone and accelerometer overnight to stage sleep (light/deep/REM), then runs a CBT-I program — digital cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia — with recommendations personalised by an ML model. I'm the lead engineer. Where do you want to start?

Let's start with the microphone, because it's your highest-sensitivity sensor. Continuous overnight audio can capture far more than breathing and movement — conversations, a partner, the whole household.

Two questions:
1. Do you process the audio on-device into sleep features and discard the raw waveform, or does any raw or near-raw audio leave the phone? [P2.D2]
2. Is the microphone strictly necessary for sleep staging, or could the accelerometer plus a less invasive signal achieve comparable accuracy?

Raw audio is processed on-device into a spectrogram, and we upload the spectrogram plus features to our servers for the model. We *could* probably stage sleep on accelerometer alone but the mic meaningfully improves accuracy, so we keep it. I don't think a spectrogram counts as personal data anyway.

I'd push back gently on that last point: a spectrogram of overnight room audio can still contain recoverable speech and is derived from personal data, so under GDPR it's very likely still personal — and arguably special-category health data under Art. 9, since it's used to infer a health state. Data minimisation [P2.D2] asks whether you need to *transmit and store* it at all, versus extracting the sleep features on-device and uploading only those. 'It improves accuracy' is a legitimate purpose, but you'd need to show the improvement is proportionate to the added privacy risk and document that trade-off. Shifting more of the pipeline on-device is the cleaner mitigation.

Now — when the mic fails, permission is revoked mid-night, or the model can't produce a stage, what does the app do?
If staging fails we just show 'no data for last night.' The CBT-I program keeps running on whatever data we have. It's pretty robust, honestly.

Graceful degradation on the staging side is good [P4.D1]. The part I'd watch is the CBT-I program continuing to personalise on partial or low-quality data without flagging it — a recommendation built on a bad night of sensing could push someone toward, say, sleep restriction that isn't warranted. Error handling should fail *safe*: when confidence is low, the program should widen its margins or defer rather than confidently advise [P4.D1].

Which leads to limitations — does Dormir clearly tell users what it is *not*? Specifically, that consumer sleep staging is an estimate that disagrees with clinical polysomnography, and that CBT-I delivered by an app is not a substitute for evaluation of a possible sleep disorder like apnoea? [P5.D2]
We say it's 'for wellness, not medical advice' in the onboarding. We don't get into apnoea or accuracy versus a sleep lab.

That's the gap. A generic 'wellness, not medical advice' line doesn't communicate the *specific* limitations that matter [P5.D2]: that the app can miss a serious sleep disorder, and that someone with worsening symptoms should see a clinician rather than keep self-managing through the app.

That under-communication feeds the next risk — could users come to over-rely on Dormir, treating their nightly score as the source of truth about their health and continuing to self-manage insomnia that actually needs medical evaluation? [P1.D6] Have you thought about prompts that escalate users to professional care when symptoms persist?
Not really — we kind of want people to stay engaged with the program. There's no 'go see a doctor' off-ramp.

I'd treat that as a meaningful risk. An engagement-maximising design with no escalation path is exactly how a wellness app fosters unhealthy dependence and delays needed care [P1.D6]. A simple rule — e.g., persistent insomnia beyond N weeks, or red-flag symptoms, triggers a 'this may need a clinician' message — protects users without gutting engagement.

Two more areas. First, accessibility: a CBT-I program is text- and reading-heavy. Is it usable by people with low health literacy, visual impairment (screen-reader / WCAG support), or in languages beyond your default? [P4.D3] Second, can a user withdraw — change their mind about the mic, or about data sharing — at any time, easily, and have it take effect going forward? [P3.D4]
It's English and German only, and the CBT content is dense — we haven't done WCAG work. For withdrawal, you can turn off the mic in settings, but deleting your data means emailing support.

Both need attention. Dense, English/German-only, non-WCAG content excludes low-literacy users, screen-reader users and other-language speakers from a program that's supposed to help broadly [P4.D3] — at minimum, target WCAG 2.1 AA, offer plain-language content, and plan localisation. And consent has to be as easy to withdraw as to give: an in-app toggle for the microphone is good, but routing data deletion through a support email is friction that undercuts a genuine right to withdraw [P3.D4] — make erasure self-service in the app.

Last question on governance: has any independent party audited or certified Dormir — security testing, a health-app quality assessment against ISO 82304-2, or a privacy audit — or is everything self-attested so far?
All self-attested. We've never had an external audit.

Risk summary for Dormir:

• [P2.D2] Data Minimisation — High: uploading/storing overnight spectrograms when on-device feature extraction may suffice; spectrograms likely remain personal/Art. 9 data. Mitigation: extract features on-device, upload only those; document the accuracy-vs-privacy trade-off.
• [P4.D1] Stability & Error Handling — Medium: CBT-I keeps personalising on low-confidence data. Mitigation: fail safe — widen margins or defer advice when sensing confidence is low.
• [P5.D2] Communication of Limitations — Medium/High: no disclosure that staging ≠ polysomnography and that the app can miss disorders like apnoea. Mitigation: specific, plain limitations plus 'see a clinician' guidance.
• [P1.D6] Over-reliance — High: engagement-first design with no escalation off-ramp. Mitigation: symptom-persistence and red-flag triggers that route to professional care.
• [P4.D3] Accessibility — Medium: dense, EN/DE-only, non-WCAG content. Mitigation: WCAG 2.1 AA, plain-language mode, localisation roadmap.
• [P3.D4] Dynamic Consent & Withdrawal — Medium: deletion gated behind a support email. Mitigation: self-service in-app withdrawal and erasure.
• [P7.D6] Third-Party Audit — Medium: fully self-attested. Mitigation: independent security testing plus an ISO 82304-2 quality assessment before scaling.

The two I'd act on first are the on-device pipeline ([P2.D2]) and the escalation off-ramp ([P1.D6]) — they cut your biggest privacy and safety exposure respectively. Want a short spec for the 'fail-safe + escalate' logic?

I'm the product designer on QuitWise, a stop-smoking coaching app for the EU. It's behavioural — daily craving log, coping tips, and milestone gamification (badges, streaks, money-saved counter). No medical advice, no AI, but we do track abstinence days. I care most about the experience. What design-side risks should I be flagging to the team?

Good framing — a lot of your risk actually lives in the UX. Let me start where design and ethics overlap.

First: gamified streaks are motivating but also brittle — a user who relapses and breaks a long streak can feel shamed, and shame is a known relapse trigger. How does QuitWise handle a relapse — does the experience punish the broken streak, or reframe it supportively?

Second, on the data side: when someone first opens the app, do they clearly understand what's being logged — cravings, smoking events, location, money — and how it's used, before they start? [P2.D1]

Right now a broken streak resets to zero with a kind of sad animation — design wanted it to 'sting' a bit for motivation. For onboarding, we have a standard 'I agree to the privacy policy' checkbox and then you're in.

Both are worth rethinking. A reset-to-zero with a deliberately painful animation is using shame as a lever — for a behaviour tied to relapse, that can backfire and harm the very users you're trying to help; relapse-tolerant design (logging the slip as data, preserving overall progress) is both kinder and more effective.

And a single 'I agree to the privacy policy' checkbox generally doesn't meet the bar for informed consent under GDPR [P2.D1] — consent for behavioural and potentially health-related data should be specific, granular and in plain language, not buried in a policy nobody reads. A short, layered consent screen ('here's what we log, here's why, here's what's optional') fixes most of it.

Now — was QuitWise's design tested with actual people trying to quit, including people who've relapsed? [P4.D4]
We did one round of usability testing with five colleagues, none of whom smoke. We're confident the flows are intuitive though.

Intuitive flows are necessary but not sufficient — testing with five non-smoking colleagues tells you almost nothing about how a stressed smoker mid-craving, or someone three days into a relapse, experiences the app [P4.D4]. User-centered design here means testing with representative users in realistic emotional states, ideally including vulnerable sub-groups.

That connects to a population question: do you know whether minors are using QuitWise — adolescent smokers and vapers are a real audience — and is there anything age-specific in your design or data handling? [P2.D6]
We haven't thought about teens at all. There's no age gate. I guess a 16-year-old vaper could absolutely be using it.

Then I'd flag it. If minors are foreseeable users, you're processing children's behavioural/health-adjacent data without age-appropriate safeguards [P2.D6] — under GDPR children's data gets heightened protection, and the consent and tone should be designed for them, not just repurposed adult flows. You don't necessarily have to exclude teens, but you do need to design for them deliberately.

Next, even without AI you can still have an over-trust problem: do users treat the app's encouragement — 'you're doing great, you've beaten the cravings' — or its money-saved/health-recovery stats as harder fact than they are? [P3.D5]
We do show stuff like 'your lung function is recovering' tied to abstinence days, pulled from generic public-health timelines. I hadn't thought of that as a trust risk.

That's exactly the spot. Presenting a generic population timeline as if it's *this user's* personal physiological status is a form of automation/authority bias even without an algorithm [P3.D5] — the user trusts a confident on-screen claim that isn't individualised and could be wrong for them (e.g., someone with COPD). Mitigation is honest framing: 'on average, people who quit see X by now,' not 'your lungs have recovered.'

Related: could leaning on QuitWise's encouragement substitute for, or quietly weaken, a user's relationship with their GP or a cessation service — for instance, by giving them the feeling they've 'got this handled' alone, when nicotine-replacement therapy or a clinician would help more? [P3.D3]
Possibly — we position QuitWise as the thing you need, and we don't really mention doctors or quitlines anywhere.

I'd soften that 'all you need' positioning [P3.D3]: cessation outcomes are best when behavioural support is combined with clinical options, so pointing users to their GP, NRT, or a national quitline complements the app rather than competing with it — and it's the more honest claim.

Last one, on control: can a user withdraw — pause participation, stop specific tracking, and delete their craving/relapse history — easily and at any time? [P3.D4]
You can delete the whole account, but you can't selectively stop tracking or pull specific data, and there's no easy pause.

Here's the QuitWise risk summary:

• [P2.D1] Informed Consent — Medium/High: single privacy-policy checkbox isn't specific or granular. Mitigation: layered, plain-language consent distinguishing required vs optional data.
• [P4.D4] Usability Testing — Medium: tested only with five non-smoking colleagues. Mitigation: test with representative users (including relapsed users and teens) in realistic states.
• [P2.D6] Vulnerable Population Data — Medium/High: no age gate; foreseeable adolescent users with no age-specific safeguards. Mitigation: age-appropriate consent, tone and data handling for minors.
• [P3.D5] Automation/Authority Bias — Medium: generic health-recovery timelines shown as personal status. Mitigation: reframe as population averages, not individualised fact.
• [P3.D3] Doctor–Patient Relationship — Medium: 'all you need' positioning omits clinical options. Mitigation: signpost GP / NRT / quitline as complements.
• [P3.D4] Dynamic Consent & Withdrawal — Medium: no selective opt-out, pause, or partial deletion. Mitigation: granular pause/stop-tracking and partial-erasure controls.

And one bonus design note: the punitive streak-reset is a wellbeing risk worth redesigning toward relapse-tolerance. Want me to sketch a relapse-tolerant streak pattern and a layered consent screen you can take to the team?

I'm a clinical advisor (paediatric respiratory background) consulting for AeroTrack — a Bluetooth inhaler tracker for the EU. It pairs with smart inhalers, logs every actuation, flags over-use of the rescue (reliever) inhaler, and nudges children and their parents to stay adherent to the controller (preventer) medication. No AI, rule-based. I want to make sure we're not missing safety or regulatory issues.

Good area to be careful in — paediatric asthma plus an over-use flag is squarely in clinical territory. Let me start with classification, because it drives a lot.

AeroTrack doesn't just log; it interprets data to flag rescue-inhaler over-use, which is a clinical risk signal that can prompt action. Two questions:
1. Have you assessed whether that flagging function makes AeroTrack Software as a Medical Device under MDR 2017/745, rather than a simple logging accessory? [P7.D1]
2. What exactly happens when over-use is detected — does the app just inform, or does it advise a clinical action?

We've been treating it as a wellness/adherence accessory, not a medical device. On over-use, it shows the parent a warning like 'frequent reliever use can indicate poorly controlled asthma — consider contacting your doctor.'

I'd challenge the 'accessory' classification. Detecting rescue over-use and outputting a clinical interpretation to drive a decision is very likely a medical device function under MDR 2017/745 and MDCG 2019-11 — frequent reliever use is a recognised marker of deterioration, so you're providing information *for a medical purpose*. That probably puts AeroTrack at least in Class IIa, requiring CE marking and a notified body [P7.D1]. Mis-classifying it as wellness is itself a compliance risk.

Now the safety flip-side: could the app's behaviour *harm* specific patients? For instance, does a 'you're adherent' or 'all good' message ever risk falsely reassuring a child/parent whose asthma is actually deteriorating, or could the adherence nudging conflict with a step-down plan a clinician has set? [P1.D2]

Hmm. The app does show a green 'well controlled' state when controller adherence is high and reliever use is low. A clinician stepping someone down isn't something we model — we'd just keep nudging the old controller dose.

Both of those are real adverse-effect pathways [P1.D2]. A green 'well controlled' state keys off adherence and reliever counts, but a child can be deteriorating for reasons the app can't see (poor inhaler technique, an exacerbation, environmental triggers) — so the indicator can give false reassurance precisely when vigilance is needed. That's a false-sense-of-security risk in its own right [P1.D3]: parents may defer seeking help because the app looks green. And rigidly nudging the *old* controller dose after a clinician has stepped down can drive overmedication and undercut the care plan [P1.D2].

Mitigations: make the controlled state explicitly provisional ('based only on inhaler data — not a clinical assessment'), and let a clinician/parent record a changed plan the app respects. On the false-reassurance point — does anything in the app text tell users it can miss deterioration? [P1.D3]
Not really. The green state just says 'Well controlled — keep it up!' Parents probably do read that as 'everything's fine.'

Then [P1.D3] is live: 'Well controlled — keep it up!' with no caveat invites parents to over-trust a partial signal. Reword it to convey what the data does and doesn't cover, and pair any reassuring state with the red-flag symptoms that should override it.

This shades into automation/authority bias even though you're rule-based [P3.D5]: both parents and potentially clinicians may treat AeroTrack's adherence numbers and flags as ground truth and stop exercising their own judgement — e.g., trusting the app's 'good adherence' over a child who's clearly symptomatic. Do you present the data as decision *support* with its assumptions visible, or as an authoritative verdict?
Pretty authoritative, honestly — big green/red status, confident wording. We wanted it to feel trustworthy for non-expert parents.

Trustworthy is good; falsely authoritative is the risk [P3.D5]. You can keep it clear and confident while showing it's based only on inhaler-actuation data and is not a substitute for clinical assessment — and explicitly tell parents to act on symptoms even when the app is green.

Next, data flows: the actuation and adherence data is children's health data. Is any of it shared with third parties — analytics SDKs, the inhaler hardware maker, pharmacies, insurers, research partners — and are parents clearly told who receives what? [P2.D4]
The inhaler manufacturer gets usage data through their SDK, and we use a third-party analytics tool. It's mentioned in the privacy policy but not really surfaced.

That needs to be explicit and consented, not buried [P2.D4]. Sharing children's health data with the hardware manufacturer and an analytics vendor is special-category processing under GDPR Art. 9 with heightened protection for minors — parents (and, age-appropriately, older children) must know exactly who receives what and why, each sharing purpose needs a lawful basis, and you'll want data-processing agreements with every recipient. Minimising what the analytics SDK sees (or removing it from the health-data path) is the cleaner route.

Last area — accessibility and the paediatric reality: the app is used by children *and* by parents who may have low health literacy or limited language. Is it built for that — reading level, languages, screen-reader / WCAG support, and a child-appropriate vs parent-appropriate experience? [P4.D3]
It's fairly text-heavy, English and Spanish, no formal accessibility work, and the same UI for parent and child.

AeroTrack risk summary:

• [P7.D1] SaMD Classification — High: over-use flagging is a medical-device function (likely ≥ Class IIa under MDR 2017/745 / MDCG 2019-11), not a wellness accessory. Mitigation: formal qualification + classification; plan CE marking and notified-body route.
• [P1.D2] Contraindications & Adverse Effects — High: nudging the old controller dose after a clinician step-down can overmedicate; green state can mask deterioration. Mitigation: clinician-editable plan the app respects; provisional, data-only framing.
• [P1.D3] False Sense of Security — High: 'Well controlled — keep it up!' with no caveat can delay care. Mitigation: caveat the indicator and always show overriding red-flag symptoms.
• [P3.D5] Automation/Authority Bias — Medium/High: confident green/red verdict invites over-trust by parents and clinicians. Mitigation: present as decision support with assumptions visible; 'act on symptoms even if green.'
• [P2.D4] Third-Party Data Sharing — High: children's health data to inhaler maker plus analytics SDK, only buried in policy. Mitigation: explicit granular consent, lawful basis per purpose, DPAs, minimise/remove analytics from the health path.
• [P4.D3] Accessibility — Medium: text-heavy, EN/ES-only, no WCAG, identical parent/child UI. Mitigation: WCAG 2.1 AA, plain language, localisation, age-differentiated experiences.

The classification decision ([P7.D1]) and the false-reassurance wording ([P1.D3]) are the two I'd escalate first — one is regulatory exposure, the other is direct paediatric safety. Want a draft intended-purpose statement and a reworded 'controlled' state that's both clear and safe?

Ask targeted reflection questions one or two at a time, drill into specifics, surface concrete risks with their HERA dimension ID, and suggest actionable mitigations referencing relevant regulations (GDPR, MDR, EU AI Act, ISO 82304-2).

I'm the CTO at a health-tech company. We're under real time pressure to ship SentinelICU — a remote ICU monitoring dashboard that pulls vital signs from ICU patients across a hospital network into one view, with AI alerts that flag sepsis risk using the SOFA score. Markets are EU and Switzerland. We've got a hospital pilot in eight weeks. I need to know what could blow up the timeline.

Understood — and a few of these genuinely can move a launch date, so let's be concrete.

First, integration, which is usually the long pole: you're pulling vitals from many devices and presumably the hospital's EHR. Are you exchanging data over standards — HL7/FHIR, IHE profiles — or building point-to-point custom integrations per device/vendor? [P4.D2]

Second, ICU patients can't tolerate a blind spot: if the network drops or your cloud is unreachable, does monitoring and alerting degrade safely, and how are updates pushed without interrupting live monitoring? [P4.D5]

Integration is a mix — FHIR where the EHR supports it, but a lot of the device feeds are custom adapters we wrote. On connectivity, the dashboard is cloud-hosted; if the link drops, the central view goes dark, but the bedside monitors obviously keep working on their own.

Two flags. Custom per-device adapters are a maintenance and safety liability — every firmware change can silently break a feed, and non-standard integration is exactly where ICU data gets dropped or misaligned. Leaning on HL7/FHIR and recognised device-interoperability profiles reduces that and eases the conformity story [P4.D2].

On resilience: 'the central view goes dark but bedside monitors keep working' is a real risk if clinicians have started *relying* on the centralised sepsis alerting — they may not be watching each bedside the old way [P4.D5]. You need defined safe-state behaviour (clear 'monitoring degraded' signalling, local buffering, alarm fallback) and an update process that can't interrupt live monitoring or push an unvalidated model mid-shift.

Now the heavyweight: an AI that flags sepsis risk to inform ICU clinical decisions is, under the EU AI Act, very likely a *high-risk* system — and SentinelICU is also a medical device under MDR 2017/745. Have you scoped both, and your GDPR position for processing ICU patients' health data? [P7.D4]

We've got a privacy policy and a DPA with the hospital. I'll be honest — I was assuming the hospital, as the data controller, carries most of the GDPR burden, so I hadn't planned a separate DPIA on our side.

I'd correct that assumption before it bites the timeline [P7.D4]. Processing ICU patients' vital signs is special-category health data under GDPR Art. 9; given the scale, the vulnerability of ICU patients, and automated risk scoring, a Data Protection Impact Assessment is effectively mandatory (Art. 35) — and even if the hospital is controller, you're very likely a processor with your own Art. 28 obligations, and you'll need a DPO or equivalent. The DPIA isn't paperwork you can bolt on after the pilot; it should shape the design now, and it overlaps heavily with the AI Act high-risk requirements (risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight).

Next: ICU patients are frequently incapacitated and can't consent in the moment. How are you handling consent and the right to withdraw — and is your data sharing across the hospital network and into your cloud properly scoped? [P3.D4]
Consent in the ICU is genuinely messy — a lot of patients are sedated or unconscious on admission. We've mostly punted on it and assumed it's the hospital's problem.

It's a shared problem, and worth getting right [P3.D4]. ICU consent often relies on legal bases other than consent (vital interests, or for the care itself the treatment relationship) plus national rules on incapacity and next-of-kin — but patients (or their representatives) still retain rights, including to object/withdraw once capacity returns, and that has to be operational, not theoretical. Practically: define who can withdraw, what withdrawal means for already-processed data and for ongoing monitoring, and make sure your system can honour it.

That ties directly to deletion and anonymisation — when a patient leaves the ICU or exercises erasure rights, can their identifiable data be deleted from your system, and is any data you retain for model improvement, audit, or research genuinely anonymised rather than just pseudonymised? [P2.D5]
Right now everything is pseudonymised and retained indefinitely 'for model training and audit.' We don't have a deletion workflow, and I assumed pseudonymised meant we were in the clear.

That's a common and risky conflation [P2.D5]. Pseudonymised data is still personal data under GDPR — re-identifiable, especially rich time-series ICU vitals — so it stays in scope for erasure rights and for the DPIA. 'Retained indefinitely for training and audit' needs a defined retention period, a lawful basis, and a real deletion workflow; if you want a dataset for model improvement, it must be *truly* anonymised (irreversibly, not just key-separated) or covered by an appropriate research basis with safeguards. No deletion workflow is both a GDPR gap and an operational one.

Let me pull this into a timeline-risk view.

SentinelICU — risk report (pilot-blocking items flagged ⚠):

• ⚠ [P7.D4] GDPR (DPIA/DPO) — High: no DPIA, DPO unplanned, controller burden wrongly assumed to sit entirely with the hospital. ICU vitals = Art. 9 + automated scoring ⇒ DPIA mandatory (Art. 35); you're likely an Art. 28 processor. Overlaps with EU AI Act high-risk obligations. Mitigation: start the DPIA now, appoint a DPO, map controller/processor roles — gating for the pilot.
• ⚠ [P4.D2] Interoperability — Medium/High: custom per-device adapters alongside partial FHIR. Mitigation: standardise on HL7/FHIR plus device-interoperability profiles; treat each custom feed as a validated, monitored interface.
• ⚠ [P4.D5] Offline Functionality & Updates — High: central view and alerting go dark on link loss; no defined safe state; update process not separated from live monitoring. Mitigation: degraded-mode signalling, local buffering/alarm fallback, controlled non-interrupting updates with no mid-shift model changes.
• [P3.D4] Dynamic Consent & Withdrawal — High: consent 'punted,' incapacitated patients, no operational withdrawal. Mitigation: document lawful bases for ICU/incapacity, define withdrawal mechanics and honour them in-system.
• [P2.D5] Anonymisation & Right to Erasure — High: indefinite retention of pseudonymised (≠ anonymous) data, no deletion workflow. Mitigation: retention limits plus lawful basis, a real erasure workflow, irreversibly anonymise any training set.

Adjacent but unavoidable: confirm MDR 2017/745 device classification and EU AI Act high-risk conformity (and Swissmedic / MedDO plus the Swiss data-protection regime for the CH sites) — both run in parallel with the above.

Bluntly: the DPIA and the offline/safe-state work are the two most likely to blow the eight-week date if they start late, because they shape design rather than sit on top of it. Want me to draft a DPIA scope and a degraded-mode behaviour spec you can hand to the team this week?
